newsitem.title: USA: U.S., Nasdaq market makers settlement approved.
newsitem.headline: U.S., Nasdaq market makers settlement approved.

text.p: U.S. district Court Judge Robert Sweet Wednesday approved a settlement of a U.S. Department of Justice antitrust suit against a group of securities firms who make markets in Nasdaq stocks.
Sweet approved a settlement that the securities firms and the government reached last July.

The settlement requires that securities firms tape record some conversations between brokers. Under terms of the settlement, the tapes cannot be used by private investors as evidence in any litigation they have against the firm. Attorneys for the private investors in a separate class action suit opposed the settlement of the Justice Department suit because of the restrictions on use of the tapes.

"We are extremely gratified that the judge upheld the landmark settlement that continues to make markets more competitive," said Department of Justice spokeswoman Gina Talamona. She said the settlement brings lower transaction costs to individual stockholders. As for the taping provision, she said "that will help us monitor the settlement."

The 24 Nasdaq market makers in the settlement include many of the biggest names on Wall Street including units of Alex. Brown Inc ; Merrill Lynch and Co Inc ; Morgan Stanley Group Inc ; Goldman, Sachs & Co; CS First Boston; Lehman Bros Holdings Inc ; PaineWebber Group Inc; Salomon Inc ; Smith Barney Inc, which is part of Travelers Group Inc ; Bear Stearns Cos Inc ; Donaldson Lufkin & Jenrette ; Dean Witter Reynolds Inc which is part of Dean Witter Discover & Co, and the securities unit of J.P. Morgan & Co Inc.
Nasdaq was not a defendant in the Justice Department suit.

In its original complaint the Department of Justice alleged that the market makers followed a "quoting convention" that was designed to deter price competition among the firms and other market makers in the trading of Nasdaq stocks.

The quoting convention resulted in the "spread" between a dealer's buying and selling price being artificially inflated. The department said that when certain buying and selling prices were changed in one-quarter point increments instead of one-eighth point, the effect was that the spread was never less than one-quarter.

"The proposed decree will have a positive impact on the public generally by deterring and permitting detection and punishment of future antitrust and securities violations on the Nasdaq market," Sweet wrote in his 32-page opinion.
Sweet said he weighed arguments for and against keeping the tapes secret and in the end decided the provision served the public interest.

Wall Street analysts said it was impossible to make a quick determination of how the profitability of firms would be affected. But one said as a rule smaller spreads mean smaller profits and vice versa.
